asc842.subject: The lease entry that most spreadsheets get wrong
asc842.body:
Quick one.

The month-1 operating lease entry trips up more controllers than the PV math does, because the expense and the liability reduction are two different numbers:

  DR  Lease Expense            5,000
  DR  Lease Liability          4,180
      CR  Cash                          5,000
      CR  Right-of-Use Asset            4,180

($5,000/month, 36 months, 6% IBR: opening liability $164,029, month-1 interest $820, so the liability drops by $4,180 and the ROU asset amortizes by the same $4,180 to keep expense straight-line.)

The full walkthrough, initial recognition through termination for both lease types:
https://kdeskaccounting.com/posts/asc-842-journal-entries/

asc606.subject: Contract term or expected customer life? The commission judgment auditors check first
asc606.body:
Quick one.

The biggest judgment in commission accounting is the amortization period, and it comes down to one question: is the renewal commission commensurate with the initial one?

  10% on new, 10% on renewal  →  amortize over the contract term
  10% on new, 2% on renewal   →  the initial commission also bought the renewals: amortize over expected customer life

Get that wrong and the deferred asset is misstated on day one. The workbook makes it a dropdown per deal (contract term / estimated benefit period / practical expedient) and documents the choice.

Full guide, with the journal entries and the rollforward your auditor asks for:
https://kdeskaccounting.com/posts/how-to-capitalize-sales-commissions-asc-606/

fixed-assets.subject: Depreciation starts when the asset is placed in service, not when the invoice posts
fixed-assets.body:
Quick one.

The most common fixed-asset finding is not the method. It is the date.

Depreciation starts when the asset is placed in service and ready for use — not the acquisition date, not the invoice date. A server bought in January and racked in March starts in March. A leasehold improvement finished in December and occupied in January starts in January, capped at the remaining lease term.

The workbook keeps acquisition and in-service dates as separate columns and caps leasehold improvements automatically.

The full guide, with the rollforward and the disposal entries:

saas-metrics.subject: Why finance should own the SaaS metrics file
saas-metrics.body:
Quick one.

Sales ops dashboards count bookings. Finance counts recognized revenue. When the two live in different tools, ARR drifts from the P&L and someone spends the last two days before the board meeting reconciling them.

Net revenue retention is the number that gets argued about most:

  NRR = (beginning MRR + expansion − contraction − churned) ÷ beginning MRR

New-customer MRR is excluded. Above 100% means the existing base grew on its own. Built from the same monthly revenue data as the financials, it reconciles instead of arguing.

The full guide:
https://kdeskaccounting.com/posts/saas-metrics-dashboard-excel/

runway.subject: Gross burn, net burn, and the runway number that actually matters
runway.body:
Quick one.

Three numbers get mixed up in every runway conversation:

  Gross burn = total monthly cash out
  Net burn   = cash out − cash in
  Runway     = cash on hand ÷ net burn

The trap is using average net burn when revenue is ramping: last quarter's average overstates runway if burn is rising and understates it if revenue is compounding. A month-by-month model with two-rate revenue growth gets the cash-zero date right; a single division does not.

The full guide:
https://kdeskaccounting.com/posts/how-to-calculate-startup-runway/
